questions.question: What broader objectives framed the design of the Majuli VR tour?
options: Enhancing user presence, covering every geographic point quickly, and maximizing tourism revenue
Capturing tangible and intangible heritage, enhancing user presence, and minimizing cyber sickness
Reducing development time, adding gaming features, and preserving real estate models
Capturing only tangible heritage, improving visual resolution, and increasing content volume
questions.explanation: The design objectives were to capture the island's tangible and intangible heritage, strengthen user presence, and reduce cyber sickness.

questions.question: Why can a large, content-rich geographic spread in the Majuli VR tour increase cyber sickness?
options: Because cultural videos are shown continuously
Because exploring that spread requires time
Because users must choose a user group before starting
Because the headset must render more textures
questions.explanation: A large, content-rich spread can cause cyber sickness if the tour is not carefully designed because exploring it takes time.

questions.question: Which process was used to develop the final design of the Majuli VR tour?
options: An iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle refined with end-user feedback and observations
A final user evaluation conducted only after the tour was finished
A guideline-based design that excluded end-user involvement
A single design phase completed before any prototype was built
questions.explanation: The final design followed the interactive system development lifecycle, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that continuously refined ideas using feedback and observations from end users.

questions.question: What informed the initial prototypes of the Majuli VR tour?
options: A standard set of navigation features unrelated to user groups
Feedback collected after the final virtual tour was released
The requirement to minimize the number of locations covered
Observed behaviors and preferences of the island's potential visitors
questions.explanation: Initial prototypes were influenced by observing the behaviors and preferences of island visitors, who were the potential users.

questions.question: Which design elements resulted from user feedback and interaction with the Majuli VR tour?
options: Pilgrim, student, and tourist icons, a video player, and information content
A curved introductory screen, a boat-ride video, and a virtual tablet
A minimap, a notification system, and user controls
Uniform illumination, high-resolution content, and ambient sounds
questions.explanation: User feedback and interaction led to design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

activities.title: Order the stages of the Majuli VR tour design process

items.title: Order the stages of the Majuli VR tour design process
steps: Objectives and design guidelines frame the design
End users provide feedback and observations
Minimap, notifications, and controls are incorporated

questions.question: In user experience design, why is identifying the users treated as the first stage?
options: So the information points can be selected through field trips.
So the platform can be chosen as device-based or web-based.
So the multimedia archive can be built before the design.
So the experience can be designed according to the users.
questions.explanation: The first stage in user experience design is to identify the users so that the experience can be designed accordingly.

questions.question: What shaped the tailored content and features of the virtual tour of the island?
options: The preferences of pilgrims, students, and tourists, collected through contextual inquiry.
The preferences of pilgrims, students, and tourists, collected only through field trips.
The preferences of device users, web users, and archive visitors, collected through contextual inquiry.
The preferences of pilgrims, students, and tourists, shown by the introductory and tutorial videos.
questions.explanation: The virtual tour's content and features were tailored to the preferences of pilgrims, students, and tourists, and those preferences were collected through contextual inquiry methods.

questions.question: Which sources helped identify the information points on the island?
options: The curved screen, introductory video, and tutorial video at the start of the tour.
The minimap, notification system, and user controls.
Interaction with users, field trips, user feedback, and the need to cover the entire island.
The boat ride video, virtual tablet interface, and ambient sounds.
questions.explanation: The information points on the island were identified based on, among other things, interaction with users, field trips, user feedback, and the need to cover the entire island.

questions.question: Why was the virtual tour designed to cover all the island's information points?
options: To shorten the navigation time and navigation path.
To keep the tour device-based rather than web-based.
To comprehensively capture the tangible and intangible heritage of the entire island.
To create a multimedia archive limited to images and videos.
questions.explanation: The virtual tour was designed to cover all 24 information points so that it could comprehensively capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of the entire island.

activities.title: Order the content-scope steps for the Majuli VR tour

items.title: Order the content-scope steps for the Majuli VR tour
steps: Users are identified for the experience
Pilgrims, students, and tourists are categorized
Information points are identified on the island
The tour is designed to cover all 24 points

questions.question: What two videos are shown on the curved screen at the starting point of the virtual tour?
options: An introductory video about Majuli and a tutorial video
A satra exploration video and a village tour video
A 360-degree boat ride video and an information point video
A tangible heritage video and an intangible heritage video
questions.explanation: The starting point uses a curved screen in an immersive setting to show an introductory video about Majuli island and a tutorial video that acquaints users with how to use the system.

questions.question: What feeling is the 360-degree boat ride video intended to create at the very start of the virtual tour?
options: The feeling of watching a curved-screen tutorial about Majuli
The feeling of walking between information points at a satra campus
The feeling of being transported by boat between two villages on the island
The feeling of being transported by boat between the mainland and the island
questions.explanation: The boat ride experience uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one bank to the other, that is, from the mainland to the island or from the island to the mainland.

questions.question: Before the actual virtual tour begins, what does the user choose, as indicated by icons?
options: A boat ride direction between the mainland and the island
A user group: pilgrims, students, or tourists
A heritage category: tangible or intangible
A starting information point on the island
questions.explanation: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

questions.question: What preprocessing steps were applied to collected images and videos to improve their visual appearance?
options: Images and videos were left unedited so that the original camera and shadow remained visible.
Only the audio tracks were cleaned while the visual content was kept exactly as captured.
Low-resolution content was used, and unwanted elements such as a 360-degree camera tripod or its shadow were added.
High-resolution content was used, and unwanted elements such as a 360-degree camera tripod or its shadow were removed.
questions.explanation: Preprocessing involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

questions.question: Why were images and videos, mostly images, edited for uniform illumination?
options: To make every image show the same weather conditions.
To let the virtual tablet choose a different light source for each place.
To reduce the need for high-resolution content.
To avoid making users feel something is odd when moving between images captured with different lighting.
questions.explanation: 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination, and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another can make the user feel that something is odd.

questions.question: How were ambient sounds incorporated into the visited places?
options: They were played depending on the place, with temple bells for a satra or religious site.
Ambient sounds were added only to the introductory video and not to the visited places.
Only birds chirping and bike horns were added, and only for villages and towns.
They were played continuously at the same volume regardless of the place.
questions.explanation: Ambient sounds such as temple bells, birds chirping, and bike horns were added and played according to the place being visited to enhance realism, with temple bells played for a satra or religious site.

questions.question: What does the virtual tablet interface provide as the main interface for users?
options: Hand-worn input, video thumbnails, and a global map
A physical controller, ambient sounds, and a local minimap
A 360-degree boat ride video, notifications, and directional arrows
Navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content
questions.explanation: The virtual tablet interface acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

questions.question: Which elements make up the navigation tools of the virtual tablet interface?
options: A left-side island map shown as a world in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map
Video thumbnails and a volume controller
A local minimap on the local interface and directional arrows
Green-highlighted 360-degree image dots and ambient sound alerts
questions.explanation: The navigation tools include a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map.

questions.question: What is the video player in the virtual tablet interface used to view?
options: A global island map and a local minimap
Cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place
A 360-degree boat ride video and ambient sounds
An introductory video and a tutorial video
questions.explanation: The video player is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

questions.question: How does the virtual tablet interface give users access to information content?
options: Through ambient sounds
Through directional arrows
Through info elements
Through video thumbnails
questions.explanation: The virtual tablet interface provides access to information content through info elements.

questions.question: Why is the virtual tablet interface designed based on real-world tablet use?
options: To reduce the need for physical controllers
To create authentic ambience at each location
To make it familiar and easy for users to use
To support wayfinding with dual maps
questions.explanation: The interface design is inspired by real-world tablet use so that it is familiar and easy for users to use.

questions.question: What role does a minimap serve for a place on the island?
options: It shows the pre-planned route for virtual-vehicle travel
It displays the entire island for global wayfinding
It gives local orientation for that specific place
It tracks the user's pose for augmented-reality registration
questions.explanation: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place and is used to give the user local orientation or a sense of belonging.

questions.question: On the local minimap, what do the white dots represent?
options: The user's current image only
The arrangement of the 360-degree images
The available cultural videos
The island's information points
questions.explanation: White dots show how the 360-degree images are arranged, while the user's current image is highlighted green.

questions.question: What happens when the user selects a navigation arrow?
options: It moves the user in a random direction along the image arrangement
It moves the user in the arrow's direction along the image arrangement
It opens the global island map on the tablet
It starts a cultural video on the tablet interface
questions.explanation: A navigation arrow indicates a direction, and selecting it moves the user in that direction along the arrangement of 360-degree images.

questions.question: Why does the system use both a global map and a local minimap?
options: To reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support
To let the user choose a virtual-vehicle destination
To register virtual content with real-world anchors
To smooth transitions between two 360-degree images
questions.explanation: The global map and local minimap are used together for location awareness, reducing clutter and giving clearer navigation support.

questions.question: How does the system indicate that a spot has something to see, such as a cultural video?
options: The current minimap dot turns green
The video player opens automatically
The information icon becomes active
A navigation arrow appears
questions.explanation: Notifications use an active information icon to alert users; selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available and can be played on the tablet interface.

questions.question: In the island tour, how does movement from one place to another happen?
options: By walking continuously through a 3D island model
By switching between two minimap views
By changing the camera position inside one image
By transitioning from one 360-degree image to another
questions.explanation: Each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

questions.question: What does view interpolation do during a transition between two 360-degree images?
options: It changes the surrounding scenes to create motion
It guides the user from one image to another
It gives the user a seated viewpoint inside a vehicle
It blurs the image boundaries to make the transition smooth and avoid jerks
questions.explanation: View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition by blurring the boundaries between two 360-degree images, preventing sudden movement or jerks.

questions.question: Why was a different travel technique required for exploring the entire island?
options: Because walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness
Because walking-based navigation is unavailable for any place on the island
Because view interpolation cannot link 360-degree images
Because the virtual vehicle cannot be selected by the user
questions.explanation: Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness.

questions.question: How does the virtual vehicle travel technique determine the movement path?
options: The system plans the path from the user's walking speed
The user selects a visible target and moves there instantly
The user selects a destination, which selects a pre-planned route
The user draws a free path for the vehicle to follow
questions.explanation: The technique is selection-based and uses pre-planned routes: the user selects a destination to select a route, not a target or an instantaneous movement.

questions.question: How does the virtual vehicle travel technique create the feeling of motion?
options: Navigation arrows point from one spot to another
View interpolation blurs the boundaries of two images
The user walks through the 360-degree images
The surrounding scenes change as the vehicle moves
questions.explanation: When the vehicle is selected, the user has a seated viewpoint inside it, and the surrounding scenes change as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion.

questions.question: In the virtual tour system's tablet interface, what can the video player let users access?
options: Textual notifications that add context about significant spots
Minimaps that provide local orientation
Directional arrows that point toward points of interest
Cultural and ecological videos, such as 360-degree, drone, or regular 2D videos
questions.explanation: The tablet video player gives access to cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location, and these videos can be 360-degree, drone, or regular 2D videos.

questions.question: How does the tablet interface make available the most relevant videos when a user is at a spot?
options: It blurs boundaries between two 360-degree images to smooth movement
It adds the material for that spot to the video list and considers user type
It lets the user select a pre-planned route for a virtual vehicle
It shows a world-in-miniature map at local information points
questions.explanation: When the user is at a spot, the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface, and the relevance of the information is also determined by user type.

questions.question: What function do textual descriptions perform in the virtual tour system?
options: They indicate which way the user should move
They create a local sense of belonging at each place
They provide additional context about locations and significant spots
They let the user select a destination for a vehicle
questions.explanation: Textual descriptions are provided as informative notifications and descriptions that add context about locations and significant spots.

questions.question: How does the virtual tour system support point-of-interest awareness?
options: With view interpolation and virtual vehicle travel
With minimaps and captured 360-degree images
With SLAM localization and matched zones
With directional arrows and information icons that provide mostly textual details
questions.explanation: Point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that guide users toward points of interest and information icons that provide further details, mostly textual, so important elements are not overlooked.

questions.question: How does the controlled navigation technique reduce cybersickness in the XR tour?
options: It removes visual cues so the user receives less sensory information.
It speeds up viewpoint changes to shorten travel time.
It uses joystick-based navigation or teleportation to prevent abrupt movements.
It encourages users to walk freely through every scene at any speed.
questions.explanation: The joystick-based controlled navigation supports smooth movement and avoids abrupt movements that can cause discomfort.

questions.question: Why must the speed of vehicular movement be chosen carefully?
options: Because slow movement always produces the most immersive feeling.
Because speed changes alter the joystick's teleported destination.
Because faster movement reduces the need for visual cues.
Because an inappropriate speed of viewpoint change can cause cybersickness.
questions.explanation: In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not carefully chosen.

questions.question: What role do consistent visual cues and smooth transitions play in the XR design?
options: They hide distant landmarks to simplify the virtual environment.
They replace joystick input with direct vehicle control.
They increase motion speed by shortening each viewpoint change.
They maintain spatial orientation and reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts.
questions.explanation: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help users keep orientation, improve awareness, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and help avoid severe cybersickness effects in the long term.

questions.question: In immersive experience design, what does the term “design” primarily refer to?
options: Audio design
Hardware design
Code design
Interface and interaction design
questions.explanation: For immersive experiences, design denotes interface and interaction design rather than code design.

two-dimensional video
tutorial video
drone video

student

controlled navigation

questions.question: How does identifying pilgrims, students, and tourists as user categories shape what a user sees in the Majuli VR tour before and during the experience?
questions.reference_answer: In user experience design, the first stage is to identify the users so the experience can be designed accordingly. The tour identifies pilgrims, students, and tourists, whose preferences were collected through contextual inquiry, and before the tour the user chooses one of these groups using icons. During the tour, the tablet interface lists videos available for the current spot, and the corresponding material is added in a way that depends on the user type, so relevant information is tailored to that user.

questions.question: How do the virtual vehicle travel technique and the dual maps address the two components of navigation in the Majuli VR tour?
questions.reference_answer: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding. The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which a route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route, allowing the user to travel in the virtual world and perceive that travel has occurred. The dual maps, made of a global map and a local minimap, support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the world in miniature and reducing clutter.

questions.question: Why is view interpolation important when a place in the Majuli VR tour is built from separate 360-degree images, and how does that choice support user comfort?
questions.reference_answer: Each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another. View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help maintain spatial orientation, reduce anxiety and sensory conflict, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.
